accroche: We are told the 1539 ordinance imposed French against regional languages. Yet its articles 110 and 111 name only “françois.”
contenu_vulgarise:
In August 1539, at his château in Villers-Cotterêts, King Francis I signs an ordinance on justice and the clergy, in 192 articles. It was registered by the Parlement of Paris on September 6. Of this whole, school history retains two articles, 110 and 111, and one sentence: French becomes the language of the administration.

## What the Text Says

Article 110 sets out the problem: the judgments of the sovereign courts must be “made and written so clearly that there is not and cannot be any ambiguity or uncertainty.” The concern is the clarity of justice.

Article 111 draws the consequence. It explains that misunderstandings have arisen from “the understanding of the Latin words” contained in the judgments, and orders that judgments and the other acts of justice be “pronounced, registered and delivered to the parties in maternal French language (*langage maternel francoys*) and not otherwise.”

Latin is therefore indeed targeted, as the language the parties do not understand. But the article names neither Occitan, nor Breton, nor any other language of the kingdom. Moreover, it concerns only justice, not the administration as a whole.

## What the Word “françois” Covers

Everything turns on these two words. For many litigants in 1539, the “maternal language” was not the king's French. The text does not settle what is to be understood by “françois.” A page from Université Laval, which reproduces the original text and its transcription, reports that the contemporaries of Francis I did not read in it the proclamation of an official language: they saw in it rather an administrative choice between the king's “françois” and the local vernacular. The expression “official language” would moreover have been foreign to them, since the word “officiel” appears in French only in 1778, according to the same page.

Whether “maternal language” designates all the mother tongues of the kingdom, or only French, jurists and linguists debate: the article does not say, and the reading “French against the patois” came after it.

## The Shift

A law is read through what the following centuries have put into it. A decree of 1794 makes French the sole language of the administration, and the ordinance of 1539 is afterward reread as the birth certificate of a language policy. The same words, before and after the Revolution, do not say the same thing. The text of 1539 remains open on what it does not say.

repere.texte: Article 111 of the ordinance signed at Villers-Cotterêts in August 1539: after noting the misunderstandings arising from the “Latin words” in judgments, it orders that acts of justice be “pronounced, registered and delivered to the parties in maternal French language (*langage maternel francoys*) and not otherwise.”
repere.source: Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts, August 1539, arts. 110-111 (Aménagement linguistique dans le monde [Language Planning in the World] website, Université Laval; text of the articles from Wikipedia)

carte.punch: 1539: the text says “maternal French language,” not “against regional languages.”
carte.idee: Article 111 of Villers-Cotterêts imposes the “langage maternel francoys” (maternal French language) in acts of justice, targeting the “Latin words” in judgments, without naming regional languages. Its contemporaries read in it an administrative choice, not an official language; the national reading comes later.

quiz.question: What does article 111 of the 1539 ordinance provide for acts of justice?
choix: That they be drafted in Latin, but translated into the vernacular if needed at the parties' request
That they be pronounced, registered and delivered to the parties in “langage maternel francoys” (maternal French language)
That they be drafted in the language of the region where the court sits, forbidding French
That they be drafted in Parisian French, to the exclusion of any other form of the language
quiz.explication: The text demands “langage maternel francoys” (maternal French language) and “not otherwise.” It targets the “Latin words” in judgments, but names no regional language and does not specify which variety of French it means: its readers in 1539 see in it an administrative choice, not an official language.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does article 110, which precedes article 111, seek?
choix: Speedy trials, by limiting the number of appeals
Clear judgments, without ambiguity or room for interpretation
The replacement of provincial judges by royal officers
The abandonment of parish registers in favor of court clerks' offices
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 110 calls for judgments that are “clear and understandable.” The concern is the intelligibility of justice for the parties, and the language of article 111 follows from it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Francis I's contemporaries not speak of an “official language”?
choix: Because the king had given up on imposing French
Because the word “officiel” only appeared in French in 1778
Because Latin remained the kingdom's only official language
Because the ordinance was annulled by the Parlement of Paris
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the Université Laval page, the word “officiel” enters French only in 1778. The notion of an official language belongs to a later rereading, and the ordinance was indeed registered by the Parlement of Paris on September 6, 1539.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which 1794 text makes French the sole language of the administration?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is a revolutionary decree of 1794, not the ordinance of 1539, that makes French the sole language of the administration. It is from this decree that the ordinance is reread as a founding act.
